questions.stem: Task Manager on a PC with a quad-core CPU that supports simultaneous multithreading (Hyper-Threading), with the feature enabled, shows how many logical processors?
questions.explanation: Simultaneous multithreading lets each physical core run two hardware threads, so 4 cores show as 8 logical processors. 4 is the physical core count with the feature off. 16 would need four threads per core, which mainstream desktop CPUs do not offer.

questions.stem: A PC gives a pattern of beeps before anything appears on the screen. Which stage of startup produced the beeps?
options: The power-on self-test (POST) run by the firmware
The operating system kernel starting its drivers
The Secure Boot signature check of the boot loader
The disk check that runs after an improper shutdown
questions.explanation: Beep codes come from POST, the firmware's hardware test that runs before any display is ready, so it signals faults such as bad memory by sound. The boot loader, the kernel and a disk check all run later and report on screen. A Secure Boot failure shows a firmware message rather than beeps.

questions.stem: Why can a 32-bit operating system normally address only about 4 GB of RAM?
options: 2 to the 32nd power is 4,294,967,296 addresses, one per byte, which is 4 GiB.
2 to the 32nd power bits equals 4 GB, and each address holds one bit.
32 address lines times 128 MB per line equals 4 GB.
Memory modules for 32-bit systems were made only up to 4 GB.
The BIOS caps 32-bit systems at 4 GB for compatibility.
questions.explanation: A 32-bit address can name 2^32 different locations, and memory is addressed by the byte, so the limit is 4,294,967,296 bytes, or 4 GiB. Counting bits instead of bytes would give only 512 MiB. The limit comes from the address width, not from module sizes or the BIOS.

questions.stem: Which commands make a Windows PC give up its DHCP-assigned IP address and request a new one?
questions.explanation: /release drops the current DHCP lease and /renew asks the DHCP server for a new one. /flushdns and /registerdns work on DNS names, not the IP lease. /all and /displaydns only display information, and netstat shows routes and connections.

questions.stem: A firewall rule allows or blocks traffic using only the source IP address and the destination TCP port, without looking at the payload. At which OSI layers does it make its decisions?
questions.explanation: IP addresses belong to the network layer (Layer 3) and TCP ports belong to the transport layer (Layer 4). Layer 2 would mean MAC addresses, and Layer 7 would mean reading the application data, which this rule never does. Layers 5 and 6 handle sessions and data formats, not addressing.

questions.stem: A host has the address 172.16.45.200/20. What is the network address of its subnet?
questions.explanation: A /20 mask is 255.255.240.0, so the third octet moves in blocks of 16: 0, 16, 32, 48. The value 45 falls in the 32 to 47 block, so the network is 172.16.32.0 and the broadcast is 172.16.47.255. 172.16.45.0 treats the mask as a /24, and 172.16.0.0 treats it as a /16.

questions.stem: A recursive DNS resolver has nothing cached and must resolve www.example.org. In what order does it query servers?
options: A root server, then a .org TLD server, then the example.org authoritative server
The example.org authoritative server, then a .org TLD server, then a root server
A .org TLD server, then a root server, then the example.org authoritative server
A root server, then the example.org authoritative server, then a .org TLD server
The client's hosts file, then a root server, then the ISP's DHCP server
questions.explanation: Resolution works from the top of the tree down: the root refers the resolver to the .org servers, which refer it to the servers authoritative for example.org, which give the answer. The resolver cannot ask the authoritative server first because it doesn't yet know where that server is. DHCP plays no part in resolving names.

questions.stem: An administrator configures a static route by hand instead of running a routing protocol. Which statement describes a real trade-off of this choice?
options: It uses no protocol bandwidth or CPU, but it does not adapt automatically if the path fails.
It adapts automatically to failures, but it uses more bandwidth than OSPF.
It is preferred over every other route, whatever the prefix length.
It must be relearned from neighbors every 30 seconds.
It can only be used for the route to the default gateway.
questions.explanation: Static routes cost nothing to maintain, but if the next hop fails they stay in place until someone changes them. Longest prefix match is still applied first, so a static route doesn't beat a more specific route. Relearning every 30 seconds describes RIP updates, and static routes can point to any network.

questions.stem: A payroll clerk with legitimate access to the pay database raises his own hourly rate. Nothing is disclosed to outsiders and the system stays online the whole time. Which security goal was violated?
questions.explanation: Integrity means data is changed only in authorized ways, and an unauthorized edit to a pay rate breaks it. Confidentiality was not broken because no one saw data they were not allowed to see, and availability was not hit because the system stayed up. Authentication worked as designed: the clerk really was who he said he was.

questions.stem: A forum shows user comments without filtering them. An attacker posts a comment containing a script that sends each reader's session cookie to his server. What is this attack?
questions.explanation: The script is saved on the site and runs in the browser of everyone who views the page, which is stored, or persistent, XSS. Reflected XSS bounces a script off the site in a single crafted request, such as a link, and is not saved. CSRF forges requests rather than running script, SQL injection targets the database, and directory traversal reaches files outside the web folder.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly tells hashing apart from encryption?
options: Hashing is one-way with a fixed-length output, while encryption can be reversed with the right key
Hashing needs a key to reverse it, while encryption does not
Hashing protects confidentiality, while encryption protects integrity
A hash grows with the size of the input, while ciphertext does not
Hashing is used only for passwords, while encryption is used only for files
questions.explanation: A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length digest that cannot be turned back into the input, while encryption is designed to be decrypted by whoever holds the key. The second option swaps the usual roles: hashes check integrity and encryption gives confidentiality. Ciphertext, not a hash, grows with the input, and both tools have many uses beyond passwords and files.

questions.stem: A unit protects a server with an edge firewall, host-based firewalls, MFA, full-disk encryption, EDR and locked server rooms, so an attacker who gets past one control still faces the others. Which principle is this?
questions.explanation: Defense in depth layers independent physical, technical and administrative controls so one failure does not expose the asset. Least privilege limits each account to the permissions its job needs, and separation of duties splits a sensitive task between people. Zero trust means never trusting a request because of its network location and verifying every access, which can use layers but is a different principle. Obscurity relies on hiding how a system works.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

a = 4
b = 7
a = a + b
b = a - b
a = a - b
print(a, b)
questions.explanation: Trace one line at a time: a becomes 11, then b becomes 11 - 7 = 4, then a becomes 11 - 4 = 7. The three lines swap the values without a temporary variable. "11 4" stops one line early, and "4 7" assumes nothing changed.

questions.stem:
In Python, what does this code print?

i = 1
s = 0
while i < 10:
    s = s + i
    i = i * 3
print(s)
questions.explanation: The condition is checked before each pass. i = 1 adds 1, i = 3 adds 3, i = 9 adds 9, then i becomes 27 and the test fails. s = 1 + 3 + 9 = 13. 40 wrongly adds 27, which is never added because the loop stops first.

questions.stem: A correct binary search, which assumes the list is sorted, is run on the unsorted list [3, 9, 1, 7, 5] to look for 9. It checks the middle item and moves left or right. What happens?
options: It reports that 9 isn't in the list, even though it is
It sorts the list first, then finds 9
It raises an error because the list is unsorted
questions.explanation: The middle item is 1, which is less than 9, so the search keeps only the right half: 7 and 5. Both are less than 9, so the range empties and it reports not found. Binary search doesn't check that its input is sorted; it just gives a wrong answer.

questions.stem:
A page has this form, and the user types cats into the box and submits it. Which request is sent?

<form action="/search" method="get">
  <input name="q">
  <button>Go</button>
</form>
options: POST /search with q=cats in the body
questions.explanation: With method="get", the browser adds the form fields to the action URL as a query string. Each field is sent as name=value, and the input's name is q, so the request is /search?q=cats. POST would put the fields in the request body instead.
